claims.reasoning: Passage [0] states this requirement verbatim.

citations.quote: All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem.

claims.reasoning: NFS is a network filesystem, and the passages state WAL does not work over a network filesystem because processes on separate hosts cannot share memory.

citations.quote: WAL does not work over a network filesystem
This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not work on a network filesystem.

claims.reasoning: Being on the same host is necessary but not sufficient: the VFS must also support version-2 shared-memory methods (unless EXCLUSIVE locking is used), otherwise opening or converting to WAL fails.

citations.quote: This means that the underlying VFS must support the "version 2" shared-memory. If the VFS does not support shared-memory methods, then the attempt to open a database that is already in WAL mode, or the attempt to convert a database into WAL mode, will fail.

claims.reasoning: Passage [2] explicitly states there can only be one writer at a time.

citations.quote: However, since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time.

claims.reasoning: Passage [2] states writers and readers can run at the same time.

citations.quote: Because writers do nothing that would interfere with the actions of readers, writers and readers can run at the same time.

claims.reasoning: BEGIN CONCURRENT is never mentioned in the passages; they only state the single-writer limit without any mechanism to lift it.

Passage [3] gives EXCLUSIVE-before-first-access as the condition for using WAL without shared memory, and passage [5] confirms that with NORMAL mode the shared-memory wal-index is required (failing without VFS shared-memory support), making EXCLUSIVE-before-first-access the only way to omit shared memory.

citations.quote: WAL databases can be created, read, and written even if shared memory is unavailable as long as the locking_mode is set to EXCLUSIVE before the first attempted access.
It is only when the shared-memory wal-index is omitted, when the locking mode is EXCLUSIVE prior to the first WAL-mode database access, that the locking mode is stuck in EXCLUSIVE.

claims.reasoning: Passage [4] states the connection remains in EXCLUSIVE mode as long as the journal mode is WAL and the only way out is to change out of WAL journal mode.

citations.quote: In that case, the database connection remains in EXCLUSIVE mode as long as the journal mode is WAL; attempts to change the locking mode using "PRAGMA locking_mode=NORMAL;" are no-ops. The only way to change out of EXCLUSIVE locking mode is to first change out of WAL journal mode.

claims.reasoning: Passage [6] states the WAL sync is omitted on commit when synchronous is NORMAL.

citations.quote: Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.

claims.reasoning: Passage [7] states this verbatim.

citations.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).

claims.reasoning: Passage [6] states writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit when synchronous is FULL.

citations.quote: Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL

claims.reasoning: The guarantee that the main thread never blocks on a sync applies only under PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, where the checkpoint is the only syncing operation. With synchronous=FULL, writers sync the WAL on every commit, so the main thread can still block on syncs; the claim's 'whatever the synchronous setting' is refuted.

citations.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation
Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL
